extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, editorial/documentary photographers, photography students and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of ethical standards and practical rules for photojournalism and editorial photography, focusing on when image alteration, staging, captioning, and editing cross ethical lines. Includes NPPA, AP, World Press Photo rules and examples of enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy as guiding principle (NPPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: As journalists we believe the guiding principle of our profession is accuracy; therefore, we believe it is wrong to alter the content of a photograph in any way that deceives the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerging electronic technologies provide new challenges to integrity; altering editorial content is a breach of NPPA ethical standards. Images affect how people think and feel about events and participants, so accuracy is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accurate and comprehensive in representation (NPPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be accurate and comprehensive in the representation of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context, avoid stereotyping individuals and groups, recognize and work to avoid presenting personal biases in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist staged photo opportunities / no staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist being manipulated by staged photo opportunities; must not intentionally contribute to, alter, or re-enact events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Press Photo: 'Must not intentionally contribute to, or alter, the scene they picture by re-enacting or staging events.' NPPA likewise warns photojournalists to resist staged opportunities. Examples: entrants or winners disqualified for arranging images; photographers fired for staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not materially alter content or context through editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images’ content and context; do not manipulate images in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes prohibition on adding/removing elements that change meaning. World Press Photo: 'Must maintain the integrity of the picture by ensuring there are no material changes to content.' Example: World Press winner disqualified for using clone stamp to remove a foot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions must be accurate and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure captions accurately describe the scene and provide appropriate context so the audience is not misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Press Photo and other organizations link caption accuracy to ethical entry rules; mismatched captions have led to controversies (e.g., caption changes on photographer websites changing meaning). Publications can be sued when photo + text combination misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability about how pictures were made
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open and transparent about the entire process through which pictures are made, and be accountable for photographic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World Press Photo requires entrants to be open about methods; verification processes (raw files, metadata) may be used. Failure to be transparent can lead to disqualification or reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pay subjects or accept gifts that influence coverage (NPPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pay sources or subjects or reward them materially for information or participation; do not accept gifts, favors, or compensation from those who might seek to influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strict ethical boundary for journalists to avoid conflicts of interest and maintain independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intentionally sabotage other journalists (NPPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not intentionally sabotage the efforts of other journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional conduct expectation; included as an ethical standard alongside accuracy and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP prohibition on adding/subtracting elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of a photograph must not be altered in PhotoShop or by any other means. No element should be digitally added to or subtracted from any photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faces or identities must not be obscured by editing. Only retouching/cloning to eliminate dust and scratches is acceptable. Examples on the page show firing/disqualification when elements were removed or composited.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP: permitted minor adjustments (cropping, dodging/burning, toning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor adjustments are acceptable: cropping, dodging and burning, conversion to grayscale, and normal toning and color adjustments limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are analogous to darkroom practices (burning/dodging). Changes that substantially alter the original scene (density, contrast, color, saturation) are not acceptable. Backgrounds should not be digitally blurred or eliminated by aggressive toning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt consult a senior photo editor (AP)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an employee has questions about the use of such methods or the AP’s requirements and limitations on photo editing, he or she should contact a senior photo editor prior to the transmission of any image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial oversight is required for borderline adjustments; this is a procedural safeguard to prevent violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Press Photo: entrants must ensure fair representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrants to the World Press Photo contest must ensure their pictures provide an accurate and fair representation of the scene they witnessed so the audience is not misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad requirement is enforced through entry rules, verification of raw files, and guidance on what counts as manipulation; 2015 example: many finalists rejected after raw-file review.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Press Photo: no material changes; editing must preserve context
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing of a picture story must provide an accurate and fair representation of its context and must not introduce material changes to content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry rules (10-13, 9) and visual examples define allowed vs disallowed edits. Violations include removing elements, compositing, or re-ordering to change meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Press Photo: verification and entry rules define manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest’s verification process and entry rules specify what counts as manipulation and how clauses of the code of ethics are enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See entry rule cross-references (e.g., clause 2 supported by entry rule 11). Examples: disqualification for arranged images or non-disclosed staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different organizations and contests have different standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Different organizations and contests have different standards for what is permissible in editing and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes varied reactions (e.g., Australian contest controversy, communication arts) — photographers should check each contest or publisher's rules before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dramatic HDR/saturation alterations that misrepresent scene
rubrics_metrics.description: HDR composites dramatically heighten saturation — these techniques may raise ethical questions when they alter perceived reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use restraint; changes in saturation or tone that substantially alter the original scene are considered unacceptable by AP and many editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/commercial requirement: label retouched commercial photos (France/GALA)
rubrics_metrics.description: French legislation requires that all altered or retouched commercial photographs of models be labelled as a retouched photograph ('photographie retouchée' / 'photo retouchée').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to commercial/advertising photography rather than journalism; the law also requires medical certificates from models about wellbeing in related French rules. Compliance is legally required where enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and consequences (disqualification, firing, revoked prizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulation, staging, or dishonest captioning can lead to firing, disqualification from contests, revocation of awards, and reputational harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites multiple examples: Brian Walski (LA Times fired for compositing), World Press Photo disqualifications, Pulitzer-linked firings, contest winners stripped of prizes.
